claim: DNA:RNA hybrids constitute a well-known source of recombinogenic DNA damage.
source: DNA:RNA hybrids constitute a well-known source of recombinogenic DNA damage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: The current literature is in agreement with DNA:RNA hybrids being produced co-transcriptionally by the invasion of the nascent RNA molecule produced in cis with its DNA template.
source: The current literature is in agreement with DNA:RNA hybrids being produced co-transcriptionally by the invasion of the nascent RNA molecule produced in cis with its DNA template.
evidence: This claim references the consensus view in existing literature.

claim: It has been suggested that recombinogenic DNA:RNA hybrids could be facilitated by the invasion of RNA molecules produced in trans in a Rad51-mediated reaction.
source: However, it has also been suggested that recombinogenic DNA:RNA hybrids could be facilitated by the invasion of RNA molecules produced in trans in a Rad51-mediated reaction.
evidence: This references a hypothesis from prior literature that the authors are testing.

claim: Unscheduled and recombinogenic DNA:RNA hybrids that trigger the SSA event are formed in cis during transcription and in a Rad51-independent manner.
source: We show that unscheduled and recombinogenic DNA:RNA hybrids that trigger the SSA event are formed in cis during transcription and in a Rad51-independent manner.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the recombination assays and genetic experiments presented in the results.

claim: No evidence was found that DNA:RNA hybrids form in trans and in a Rad51-dependent manner.
source: We found no evidence that such hybrids form in trans and in a Rad51-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a negative finding supported by the lack of recombination enhancement when RNA is produced in trans.

claim: R loops are structures formed by a DNA:RNA hybrid and the complementary displaced single stranded DNA (ssDNA).
source: R loops are structures formed by a DNA:RNA hybrid and the complementary displaced single stranded DNA (ssDNA).
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established knowledge.

claim: R loops were observed naturally as programmed events in specific genomic sites such as the S regions of Immunoglobulin genes in mammals or mitochondrial DNA.
source: They were observed naturally as programmed events in specific genomic sites such as the S regions of Immunoglobulin genes in mammals or mitochondrial DNA (Chang et al., 1985; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Yu et al., 2003), where they play specific functions by promoting class switch recombination or DNA replication, respectively
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: R loops play specific functions by promoting class switch recombination or DNA replication in Immunoglobulin genes and mitochondrial DNA respectively.
source: They were observed naturally as programmed events in specific genomic sites such as the S regions of Immunoglobulin genes in mammals or mitochondrial DNA (Chang et al., 1985; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; Yu et al., 2003), where they play specific functions by promoting class switch recombination or DNA replication, respectively
evidence: This functional role is supported by cited literature.

claim: Unscheduled non-programmed R loop structures form upon dysfunction of RNA binding proteins involved in the assembly or processing and export of the protein-mRNA particle (mRNP) such as the THO complex or the SRSF1 splicing factor.
source: but also as unscheduled non-programmed structures upon dysfunction of RNA binding proteins involved in the assembly or processing and export of the protein-mRNA particle (mRNP) such as the THO complex or the SRSF1 splicing factor (Huertas and Aguilera, 2003; Li and Manley, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: R loops have been inferred in the rDNA regions of the bacterial chromosome upon Topo I inactivation.
source: Also, they have been inferred in the rDNA regions of the bacterial chromosome upon Topo I inactivation (Drolet et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: R loops are detected from yeast to humans in many transcribed regions of the eukaryotic genome in wild-type cells.
source: Accumulated evidence indicates that R loops are detected from yeast to humans in many transcribed regions of the eukaryotic genome in wild-type cells, in cells defective in several metabolic processes covering from RNA processing to DNA replication and repair and in cells deficient in specific chromatin factors (Bhatia et al., 2014; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; García-Rubio et al., 2015; Herrera-Moyano et al., 2014; Mischo et al., 2011; Paulsen et al., 2009; Schwab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: R loops are detected in cells defective in several metabolic processes covering from RNA processing to DNA replication and repair.
source: Accumulated evidence indicates that R loops are detected from yeast to humans in many transcribed regions of the eukaryotic genome in wild-type cells, in cells defective in several metabolic processes covering from RNA processing to DNA replication and repair and in cells deficient in specific chromatin factors (Bhatia et al., 2014; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; García-Rubio et al., 2015; Herrera-Moyano et al., 2014; Mischo et al., 2011; Paulsen et al., 2009; Schwab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: R loops are detected in cells deficient in specific chromatin factors.
source: Accumulated evidence indicates that R loops are detected from yeast to humans in many transcribed regions of the eukaryotic genome in wild-type cells, in cells defective in several metabolic processes covering from RNA processing to DNA replication and repair and in cells deficient in specific chromatin factors (Bhatia et al., 2014; García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019; García-Rubio et al., 2015; Herrera-Moyano et al., 2014; Mischo et al., 2011; Paulsen et al., 2009; Schwab et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The biological consequences of R loop structures include replication stress, DNA breaks and genome instability that can be detected as hyperrecombination, plasmid loss or gross chromosomal rearrangements.
source: The biological consequences of such R loop structures are diverse and include replication stress, DNA breaks and genome instability that can be detected as hyperrecombination, plasmid loss or gross chromosomal rearrangements (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids have been inferred by their potential to induce DNA damage and recombination.
source: Indeed, DNA:RNA hybrids have been inferred by their potential to induce DNA damage and recombination, but they can also be directly detected via different methodologies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about detection methods.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids can be directly detected via electrophoresis detection after nuclease treatment, bisulfite mutagenesis or either in situ immunofluorescence or DNA:RNA Immuno-Precipitation (DRIP) using the S9.6 anti-DNA:RNA monoclonal antibody.
source: These include electrophoresis detection after nuclease treatment, bisulfite mutagenesis or either in situ immunofluorescence or DNA:RNA Immuno-Precipitation (DRIP) using the S9.6 anti-DNA:RNA monoclonal antibody (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019).
evidence: This describes established methodologies cited from prior work.

claim: Most DNA:RNA hybrids are compatible with a co-transcriptional formation.
source: The increasing number of reports showing R loop accumulation in different organisms from bacteria to human cells, and the relevance of their functional consequences, whether on genome integrity, chromatin structure and gene expression suggest that most DNA:RNA hybrids are compatible with a co-transcriptional formation (García-Muse and Aguilera, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from accumulated evidence in the literature.

claim: It is the RNA produced in cis that invades the duplex DNA, a reaction that can be facilitated by DNA sequence and supercoiling.
source: This is consistent with the idea that it is the RNA produced in cis the one that invades the duplex DNA, a reaction that can be facilitated by DNA sequence and supercoiling (Stolz et al., 2019) as well as by nicking of the DNA template (Roy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrid formation can be facilitated by nicking of the DNA template.
source: This is consistent with the idea that it is the RNA produced in cis the one that invades the duplex DNA, a reaction that can be facilitated by DNA sequence and supercoiling (Stolz et al., 2019) as well as by nicking of the DNA template (Roy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The evidence of DNA:RNA hybrid formation at breaks has matured in the last years.
source: The evidence of DNA:RNA hybrid formation at breaks has matured in the last years (Cohen et al., 2018; D'Alessandro et al., 2018; Li et al., 2016; Ohle et al., 2016; Teng et al., 2018; Yasuhara et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: The source and role of DNA:RNA hybrids at breaks remains controversial.
source: although the source and role of such hybrids remains still controversial (Aguilera and Gómez-González, 2017; Puget et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating ongoing debate in the literature.

claim: Some researchers claim that DNA:RNA hybrids detected around DNA breaks mostly accumulate at transcribing sites, in agreement with their co-transcriptional formation.
source: Whereas some claim that DNA:RNA hybrids detected around DNA breaks mostly accumulate at transcribing sites (Cohen et al., 2018), in agreement with their co-transcriptional formation
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Some researchers suggest that there is no preference for DNA:RNA hybrids to form at transcribed loci in human cells.
source: others suggest that there is no preference for DNA:RNA hybrids to form at transcribed loci in human cells (D'Alessandro et al., 2018), implying a scenario in which DNA:RNA hybrids at break sites would form either de novo or with RNAs produced at different loci (in trans).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Short RNAs can be used as templates for the recombinational repair of DSBs in a reaction catalyzed by Rad52 in yeast.
source: Moreover, it has been shown in yeast that short RNAs can be used as templates for the recombinational repair of DSBs in a reaction catalyzed by Rad52 (Keskin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids can form in vitro with the aid of the bacterial DNA strand exchange protein RecA.
source: DNA:RNA hybrids can also form in vitro with the aid of the bacterial DNA strand exchange protein RecA (Kasahara et al., 2000; Zaitsev and Kowalczykowski, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids are formed with RNAs produced in trans as intermediates in the course of ribonucleoprotein-mediated reactions such as telomerase and CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein involved in specific reactions.
source: In vivo, DNA:RNA hybrids are formed with RNAs produced in trans as intermediates in the course of ribonucleoprotein-mediated reactions such as telomerase and CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein involved in specific reactions (Collins, 2000; Jinek et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids have been reported to have regulatory roles in gene expression when formed by long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) at in trans loci such as the cases of the GAL lncRNA in yeast or the APOLO lncRNA in plants.
source: They have also been reported to have regulatory roles in gene expression when formed by long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) at in trans loci such as the cases of the GAL lncRNA in yeast (Cloutier et al., 2016) or the APOLO lncRNA in plants (Ariel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: It was inferred that DNA:RNA hybrids could be formed with RNAs produced in trans by a reaction catalyzed by the eukaryotic DNA strand exchange protein Rad51 in S. cerevisiae.
source: By S9.6 immunofluorescence (IF) and a yeast artificial chromosome-based genetic assay that measures gross chromosomal rearrangements, it was inferred that DNA:RNA hybrids could be formed with RNAs produced in trans by a reaction catalyzed by the eukaryotic DNA strand exchange protein Rad51 (Wahba et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from prior work that the authors are testing.

claim: The S9.6 antibody can also recognize dsRNAs.
source: Nevertheless, the fact that the detected gross chromosomal rearrangements could depend on Rad51 and that the S9.6 antibody can also recognize dsRNAs (Hartono et al., 2018; König et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The bacterial LacZ gene consists of a 3 Kb sequence with high G+C content previously reported to be hyper-recombinant and difficult to transcribe in DNA:RNA hybrid-accumulating strains, such as tho mutants.
source: The bacterial LacZ gene consists of a 3 Kb sequence with high G+C content previously reported to be hyper-recombinant and difficult to transcribe in DNA:RNA hybrid-accumulating strains, such as tho mutants (Chávez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The GL-LacZ recombination system is a leu2 direct-repeat construct carrying the LacZ gene in between and under the GAL1 inducible promoter so that this construct is transcribed as a single RNA unit driven from the GAL1 promoter.
source: The GL-LacZ recombination system is a leu2 direct-repeat construct carrying the LacZ gene in between and under the GAL1 inducible promoter so that this construct is transcribed as a single RNA unit driven from the GAL1 promoter (Piruat and Aguilera, 1998).
evidence: This describes the experimental system used, with citation to prior work.

claim: Single-Strand Annealing (SSA) events cause the deletion of the LacZ sequence and one of the leu2 repeats leading to Leu+ recombinants in a Rad51-independent manner.
source: Single-Strand Annealing (SSA) events cause the deletion of the LacZ sequence and one of the leu2 repeats leading to Leu+ recombinants in a Rad51-independent manner (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the assay, referencing Figure 1A and citing prior knowledge.

claim: The stimulation of transcription in cis elevated the frequency of recombination threefold in wild-type cells.
source: The analysis of recombination in wild-type cells revealed that whereas the stimulation of transcription in cis elevated the frequency of recombination threefold
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The stimulation of transcription in trans driven from the tetp:LacZ construct had no effect on recombination in wild-type cells.
source: the stimulation of transcription in trans driven from the tetp:LacZ construct had no effect on recombination (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Homologous transcripts coming from a different locus do not represent a detectable source of genetic instability in wild-type conditions.
source: These results already suggest that homologous transcripts coming from a different locus do not represent a detectable source of genetic instability in wild-type conditions
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the recombination data.

claim: mRNA coating protects DNA from co-transcriptional RNA hybridization.
source: However, it is known that mRNA coating protects DNA from co-transcriptional RNA hybridization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: mft1∆ and hpr1∆ enhanced recombination slightly when transcription in cis was switched off, likely as a consequence of leaky transcription from the GAL1 promoter in glucose.
source: mft1∆ and hpr1∆ enhanced recombination slightly when transcription in cis was switched off (Figure 2A), likely as a consequence of leaky transcription form the GAL1 promoter in glucose (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays with an interpretation based on transcription data.

claim: Recombination frequencies rocketed when transcription was stimulated in cis in mft1∆ and hpr1∆ mutants, in agreement with previous reports.
source: More significantly and in agreement with previous reports (Chávez et al., 2000), recombination frequencies rocketed when transcription was stimulated in cis.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Transcription activation in trans did not enhance recombination in mft1∆ and hpr1∆ mutants.
source: However, transcription activation in trans did not enhance recombination, as it would be expected if additional DNA:RNA hybrids could form with RNA produced in trans.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Under conditions of high transcription of the recombination system (transcription in cis), RNA driven from an ectopic locus (transcription in trans) led to a partial suppression of the hyper-recombination.
source: Instead, under conditions of high transcription of the recombination system (transcription in cis), RNA driven from an ectopic locus (transcription in trans) led to a partial suppression of the hyper-recombination.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A DNA:RNA hybrid produced in the template DNA strand can impair transcription elongation.
source: Given that a DNA:RNA hybrid produced in the template DNA strand can impair transcription elongation (Tous and Aguilera, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The production of RNAs in trans from the tet::LacZ construct led to a reduction of the hyper-recombination in the GL-LacZi system.
source: Surprisingly, the production of RNAs in trans from the tet::LacZ construct also led to a reduction of the hyper-recombination in this system.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the GL-LacZi system, the suppression of hyper-recombination by trans RNA was stronger and was also observed in glucose, when transcription in cis was off.
source: Furthermore, in this case, the suppression was stronger and was also observed in glucose, when transcription in cis was off.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the GL-LacZi scenario, the RNA produced in trans is complementary to the mRNA produced in cis, so they can hybridize together forming a dsRNA that would preclude the possibility to form DNA:RNA hybrids at the GL-LacZi construct.
source: This could be explained because, in this scenario, the RNA produced in trans is complementary to the mRNA produced in cis. Consequently, they can hybridize together forming a dsRNA that would preclude the possibility to form DNA:RNA hybrids at the GL-LacZi construct.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the data.

claim: Transcription from the long LacZ gene is inefficient and leads to unstable RNA products, particularly in tho mutants.
source: Since transcription from the long LacZ gene is inefficient and leads to unstable RNA products, particularly in tho mutants (Chávez et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: With the tetp:LacZ400 construct, no suppression of the tho-induced hyper-recombination by the production of RNA in trans was observed.
source: Strikingly, in this case, we observed no suppression of the tho-induced hyper-recombination by the production of RNA in trans.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Recombination frequencies were not significantly enhanced by transcription in trans in any of the strains or conditions tested with the tetp:LacZ400 construct.
source: More importantly and again, recombination frequencies were not significantly enhanced by transcription in trans in any of the strains or conditions tested, further arguing against mRNA produced in trans as a possible source of recombinogenic DNA:RNA hybrids.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The THO complex is thought to prevent R-loops mainly by promoting a proper mRNA-protein assembly.
source: The THO complex is thought to prevent R-loops mainly by promoting a proper mRNA-protein assembly (Luna et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The two RNase H enzymes efficiently degrade the RNA moiety of DNA:RNA hybrids once formed.
source: whereas the two RNase H enzymes efficiently degrade the RNA moiety of DNA:RNA hybrids once formed (Cerritelli and Crouch, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells elevated the recombination frequency when transcription was stimulated in cis.
source: Figure 2A and C show that rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells elevated the recombination frequency when transcription was stimulated in cis, as expected.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: The recombination frequencies in rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells were not altered by producing transcripts in trans.
source: Importantly, the recombination frequencies were not altered by producing transcripts in trans, arguing again against the recombinogenic potential of putative DNA:RNA hybrids formed with RNAs produced in trans.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids accumulate in both hpr1∆ and rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutants in all GL-LacZ, tet:LacZ and GL:lacZi sequences.
source: In order to confirm DNA:RNA hybrid formation in these different sequence contexts, we performed DRIP experiments at the LacZ sequence (Figure 3) and we observed that DNA:RNA hybrids accumulate in both, hpr1∆ and rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutants, and in all GL-LacZ, tet:LacZ and GL:lacZi sequences as expected
evidence: This is a result from DRIP experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Transcription at the TL-LacZ recombination system enhanced recombination as previously published.
source: Figure 4 shows that, whereas transcription at the TL-LacZ recombination system enhanced recombination as previously published (Santos-Pereira et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 4, with citation to prior work.

claim: No significant stimulation of recombination was detected when RNAs were produced in trans in either wild-type, hpr1∆ or rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells even when the RNA was generated from the strong GAL1 promoter in the TL-LacZ system.
source: again no significant stimulation of recombination was detected when RNAs were produced in trans in either wild-type, hpr1∆ or rnh1∆ rnh201∆ cells even when the RNA was generated from the strong GAL1 promoter.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transcription of the chromosomal recombination system promoted a 30-fold increase in recombination levels in the tho mutant hpr1∆ with respect to the WT.
source: As it can be seen in Figure 5, transcription of the chromosomal recombination system promoted a 30-fold increase in recombination levels in the tho mutant hpr1∆ with respect to the WT, in agreement with all previous data showing that co-transcriptional DNA:RNA hybrids are a potent source of recombination.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: mRNA produced at a different locus had no effect on recombination, neither in wild-type cells nor in the tho mutant hpr1∆ in the chromosomal GL-LacZ system.
source: By contrast, mRNA produced at a different locus had no effect on recombination, neither in wild-type cells nor in the tho mutant hpr1∆.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: RNA produced at a particular locus does not lead to recombinogenic DNA damage at regions located in trans.
source: Hence, altogether, these results argue that, in contrast to mRNA produced in cis, RNA produced at a particular locus does not lead to recombinogenic DNA damage at regions located in trans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recombination data across multiple experiments.

claim: The recombination events detected in the direct-repeat systems are deletions occurring by SSA between direct repeats, which do not require Rad51.
source: It is important to remark that the recombination events detected in our assays are deletions occurring by SSA between direct repeats, which do not require Rad51 (Pardo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RAD51 deletion caused no significant changes in the recombination frequencies in the SSA assay.
source: Indeed, in agreement with SSA annealing being Rad51-independent, RAD51 deletion caused no significant changes in the recombination frequencies in our assay.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: No differences in recombination were observed when RAD51 was deleted in hpr1∆ cells even when the LacZ sequence was expressed from the plasmid containing the tet::LacZ construct.
source: Importantly, we observed no differences when RAD51 was deleted in hpr1∆ cells even when the LacZ sequence was expressed from the plasmid containing the tet::LacZ construct.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The result argues against Rad51 facilitating or impeding the formation of DNA:RNA hybrids with RNAs produced in trans.
source: This result argues against Rad51 facilitating or impeding the formation of DNA:RNA hybrids with RNAs produced in trans.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the recombination data.

claim: The absence of Rad51 had no effect on the hyper-recombination observed in hpr1∆ cells when transcription was induced in cis.
source: As shown in Figure 6, the absence of Rad51 had no effect on the hyper-recombination observed, as hpr1∆ rad51∆ cells elevated the recombination frequency more than 70-fold with respect to rad51∆, similarly to Rad51+ cells.
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: The in cis DNA:RNA hybrid-mediated hyper-recombination phenotype is independent of Rad51.
source: This result clearly indicates that the in cis DNA:RNA hybrid-mediated hyper-recombination phenotype is actually independent on Rad51.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recombination data in Figure 6.

claim: hpr1∆ caused an increase in Rad52 foci that was enhanced by AID overexpression and suppressed by RNase H overexpression.
source: In agreement with the role of the THO complex in R loop prevention, hpr1∆ caused an increase in Rad52 foci that was enhanced by AID overexpression and suppressed by RNase H overexpression, as previously reported (Alvaro et al., 2007; García-Pichardo et al., 2017; Wellinger et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a result from the Rad52-YFP foci analysis shown in Figure 7A, with citations to prior work.

claim: The accumulation of Rad52 foci observed in rad51∆ cells was not affected by either AID or RNase H overexpression.
source: By contrast, the accumulation of Rad52 foci observed in rad51∆ cells was not affected by either AID or RNase H overexpression.
evidence: This is a result from the Rad52-YFP foci analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: R loops are not the cause for the genetic instability observed in the absence of Rad51.
source: This result argues that R loops are not the cause for the genetic instability observed in the absence of Rad51.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Rad52 foci data.

claim: The accumulation of Rad52 foci in rad51∆ cells is likely due to the accumulation of unrepaired recombination intermediates.
source: The accumulation of Rad52 foci in rad51∆ cells is rather likely due to the accumulation of unrepaired recombination intermediates, as previously suggested (Alvaro et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: hpr1∆ rad51∆ cells showed a similar result to rad51∆ cells in Rad52 foci accumulation, supporting that the accumulation of recombinogenic damage in hpr1∆ cells is independent of Rad51.
source: Importantly, hpr1∆ rad51∆ cells showed a similar result, further supporting that the accumulation of recombinogenic damage in hpr1∆ cells is independent on Rad51.
evidence: This is a result from the Rad52-YFP foci analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The number of cells with S9.6 positive signal was similar in hpr1∆ and in hpr1∆ rad51∆ cells.
source: Figure 7B illustrates that the number of cells with S9.6 positive signal was similar in hpr1∆ and in hpr1∆ rad51∆ cells.
evidence: This is a result from the S9.6 immunofluorescence on metaphase spreads shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The Rad51 protein is not required for the DNA:RNA hybrid formation previously reported in THO mutants.
source: Altogether, these results demonstrate that the Rad51 protein is not required for the DNA:RNA hybrid formation previously reported in THO mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Rad52 foci and S9.6 immunofluorescence data.

claim: SSA events are Rad51-independent and do not require DNA strand exchange, but just annealing between resected single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) for which the action of Rad52 is sufficient.
source: It is well established that SSA events are Rad51-independent; they do not require DNA strand exchange, but just annealing between resected single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) for which the action of Rad52 is sufficient (Figure 1A; Pardo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to prior work.

claim: In contrast to the RNA produced at the site where SSA occurs, an RNA produced in a remote locus does not induce an increase in homology-directed repair.
source: Our constructs show that, in contrast to the RNA produced at the site where SSA occurs, an RNA produced in a remote locus does not induce an increase in homology-directed repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recombination data across multiple experiments.

claim: Recombination is not induced by in trans RNA production even when the major DNA:RNA removal machinery is absent (rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutant) or when the RNA coating functions preventing DNA:RNA hybrid formation are impaired (tho mutants).
source: Importantly, recombination is not induced by in trans RNA production even when the major DNA:RNA removal machinery is absent (rnh1∆ rnh201∆ mutant) or when the RNA coating functions preventing DNA:RNA hybrid formation are impaired (tho mutants), arguing against the idea that harmful DNA:RNA hybrids could spontaneously form in trans and constitute a menace for genome integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recombination data across multiple experiments.

claim: Co-transcriptional R-loops are responsible for the hyper-recombination of hpr1∆.
source: Co-transcriptional R-loops are responsible for the hyper-recombination of hpr1∆ as reported previously (Huertas and Aguilera, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The free RNA itself, and not in the form of DNA:RNA hybrids formed at the template DNA strand, plays some role in preventing the hyper-recombination.
source: The fact that this suppressor effect was augmented when one of the LacZ sequences was inverted (Figure 2B) and prevented by a shorter LacZ construct (Figure 2C), which was reported to be more stable in tho mutant backgrounds (Chávez et al., 2001), suggests that the free RNA itself, and not in the form of DNA:RNA hybrids formed at the template DNA strand, plays some role in preventing the hyper-recombination, likely because stable RNAs can interfere with transcription at a homologous locus.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the recombination data from Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: No suppressor effect was observed when the recombination system was placed in a chromosome or when the ectopic RNA was transcribed from the GAL1 promoter.
source: However, no suppressor effect was observed when the recombination system was placed in a chromosome (Figure 5) or when the ectopic RNA was transcribed from the GAL1 promoter (Figures 2 and 4).
evidence: This is a result from the recombination assays shown in Figures 2, 4, and 5.

claim: DNA:RNA hybrids formed with an RNA produced in trans were previously suggested to threaten genome integrity.
source: DNA:RNA hybrids formed with an RNA produced in trans were previously suggested to threaten genome integrity (Wahba et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from prior work that the authors are discussing.

claim: Recombination involving multiple substrates was first reported in S. cerevisiae, in which an induced-DSB triggered recombination between two other homologous fragments at different chromosomes.
source: Recombination involving multiple substrates was first reported in S. cerevisiae, in which an induced-DSB triggered recombination between two other homologous fragments at different chromosomes (Ray et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Tri-parental recombination assays have been successfully used to define specific features of the HR reaction as well as for studies of Break-Induced Recombination (BIR) or translocations and chromosomal rearrangements occurring between ectopic regions.
source: Tri-parental recombination assays have been successfully used since then to define specific features of the HR reaction as well as for studies of Break-Induced Recombination (BIR) or translocations and chromosomal rearrangements occurring between ectopic regions (Pardo and Aguilera, 2012; Piazza et al., 2017; Ruiz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The assay used to infer the potential of DNA:RNA hybrids formed with RNAs produced in trans to induce genetic instability does not exclude the possibility that the RNA forms the hybrid in cis inducing subsequently a DSB that would stimulate the recombination events studied.
source: Hence, the assay used to infer the potential of DNA:RNA hybrids formed with RNAs produced in trans to induce genetic instability (Wahba et al., 2013) relied on an RNA fragment produced at a (first) DNA region that could form a DNA:RNA hybrid with a (second) ectopic homologous DNA region that would promote its deletion or loss, leading to a genetically detectable phenotype. Thus, this assay does not exclude the possibility that the RNA forms the hybrid in cis inducing subsequently a DSB that would stimulate the recombination events studied (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a critical interpretation of prior work.

claim: The increased genetic instability observed in the Wahba et al. study could be explained by the invasion of the 3' end of a DNA break induced by the DNA:RNA hybrid formed at the first site rather than implying that Rad51 is required for the RNA to invade the second DNA sequence.
source: Indeed, this event would demand the action of Rad51 for DNA strand invasion, consistent with the results obtained (Wahba et al., 2013). Therefore, the increased genetic instability observed could be explained by the invasion of the 3' end of a DNA break induced by the DNA:RNA hybrid formed at the first site (Figure 8) rather than implying that Rad51 is required for the RNA to invade the second DNA sequence.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of prior work, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The hyper-recombinogenic potential of DNA:RNA hybrids is Rad51-independent.
source: In our case, however, we show that the hyper-recombinogenic potential of DNA:RNA hybrids is Rad51-independent (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recombination data shown in Figure 6 (note: the text says Figure 4 but likely refers to Figure 6 based on context).

claim: Recombination between the leu2 repeats could be originated by either a DNA:RNA hybrid in cis or by a DSB occurring in between the repeats, or by a bypass mechanism involving template switching.
source: Recombination between the leu2 repeats could be originated by either a DNA:RNA hybrid in cis or by a DSB occurring in between the repeats, or as suggested previously for tho mutants, by a bypass mechanism involving template switching (Gómez-González et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a discussion of possible mechanisms, with citation to prior work.

claim: The initial lesion triggered by a hybrid could be a nick or ssDNA gap, as previously proposed for tho mutants.
source: It is worth noting that although we are depicting the SSA reactions as being initiated by a DSB (Figures 1 and 8), we cannot discard that the initial lesion triggered by a hybrid is a nick or ssDNA gap, as previously proposed for tho mutants (Gómez-González et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation, with citation to prior work.

claim: A DSB occurring at the locus where the RNA in trans was generated could give rise to Leu+ recombinants in the assay, but such recombination events would be Rad51-dependent.
source: Similarly, a DSB occurring at the locus where the RNA in trans was generated could give rise to Leu+ recombinants in our assay. However, such recombination events would be Rad51-dependent, as they will require a Rad51-dependent invasion into the GL-LacZ construct (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a logical inference about the mechanism, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The Leu+ recombinants obtained in rad51∆ mutant cells can only be explained by Rad51-independent events occurring in cis, at the GL-LacZ construct.
source: Hence, the Leu+ recombinants obtained in rad51∆ mutant cells (Figure 5) can only be explained by Rad51-independent events occurring in cis, at the GL-LacZ construct.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the recombination data in Figure 6 (note: text says Figure 5 but likely refers to Figure 6).

claim: The fact that no significant increase in Leu+ recombinants was detected by inducing transcription in trans, either in RAD51 or rad51∆ backgrounds, rules out the possibility that recombinogenic DNA:RNA hybrids form in trans in the assay.
source: Strikingly, the fact that we detected no significant increase in Leu+ recombinants by inducing transcription in trans, either in RAD51 or rad51∆ backgrounds rules out the possibility that recombinogenic DNA:RNA hybrids form in trans in our assay.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the recombination data.

claim: S9.6 signal detected by IF was reduced by rad51∆ in metaphase spreads in a previous study.
source: It was previously shown that S9.6 signal detected by IF was reduced by rad51∆ in metaphase spreads (Wahba et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a claim from prior work that the authors are contrasting with their results.

claim: S9.6 signal was detected in metaphase spreads of the hpr1∆ mutant of the THO complex in both RAD51 and rad51∆ backgrounds in this study.
source: By contrast, we detected S9.6 signal in metaphase spreads of the hpr1∆ mutant of the THO complex in both RAD51 and rad51∆ backgrounds (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a result from the S9.6 immunofluorescence shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The S9.6 antibody also recognizes dsRNA.
source: The uncertainty about the identity of the structures detected by IF using the S9.6 antibody, which also recognizes dsRNA (Hartono et al., 2018; König et al., 2017; Silva et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Chromosomal spreads could preferentially visualize the rDNA regions, in which high levels of dsRNA structures formed by the rRNAs exist.
source: and the possibility that chromosomal spreads could preferentially visualize the rDNA regions, in which high levels of dsRNA structures formed by the rRNAs, makes difficult to make conclusions on S9.6 IFs in this case.
evidence: This is a speculation about technical limitations.

claim: No evidence was found for a Rad51-facilitated strand invasion from RNAs produced in trans.
source: Thus, we have found no evidence for a Rad51-facilitated strand invasion from RNAs produced in trans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: None of the so far reported DNA:RNA hybrid interactomes has identified RAD51.
source: Further arguing against any major role of this recombinase in R loop metabolism or function, none of the so far reported DNA:RNA hybrid interactomes has identified RAD51 (Cristini et al., 2018; Nadel et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior interactome studies.

claim: RecA can catalyze an inverse DNA strand exchange reaction with DNA or RNA thus promoting the assimilation of a transcript into duplex DNA in vitro.
source: The fact that, in vitro, RecA can catalyze an inverse DNA strand exchange reaction with DNA or RNA thus promoting the assimilation of a transcript into duplex DNA (Kasahara et al., 2000; Zaitsev and Kowalczykowski, 2000) does not argue that this is the case for unscheduled recombinogenic R loops in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: The biological significance of RecA-mediated DNA:RNA hybridization likely relies on its use for replication initiation of prokaryotic cells.
source: More likely, the biological significance of this process relies on its use for replication initiation of prokaryotic cells as originally proposed (Zaitsev and Kowalczykowski, 2000)
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RecA-mediated DNA:RNA hybridization may be used for replication-dependent recombination to restart stalled forks.
source: for replication-dependent recombination to restart stalled forks (Pomerantz and O'Donnell, 2008)
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: RecA-mediated DNA:RNA hybridization may be used for transcription-induced origin-independent replication.
source: or even for transcription-induced origin-independent replication (Stuckey et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: DNA:RNA hybridization could occur in trans under regulated conditions but not spontaneously as unscheduled and harmful structures that would put genome integrity into risk.
source: Hence, DNA:RNA hybridization could occur in trans under regulated conditions but not spontaneously as unscheduled and harmful structures that would put genome integrity into risk.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and literature review.

claim: The assimilation of a transcript into a duplex DNA in trans would be tightly regulated and limited to specific reactions such as the case of telomerase or CRISPR and possibly other proteins yet to be discovered.
source: Thus, the assimilation of a transcript into a duplex DNA in trans would be tightly regulated and limited to specific reactions such as the case of telomerase or CRISPR and possibly other proteins yet to be discovered.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known examples.

claim: For the case of the GADP45 factor that binds to promoters harboring hybrids formed by lncRNAs, it is unclear whether such hybrids are formed in trans and in a GADP45-dependent manner.
source: For other cases, such as that of the GADP45 factor that binds to promoters harboring hybrids formed by lncRNAs (Arab et al., 2019), it is unclear whether such hybrids are formed in trans and in a GADP45-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a statement of uncertainty about a specific case, with citation.

claim: RNAs do not form hybrids in trans, so that the previously reported induction of Rad51-dependent ectopic genetic instability would be explained by R loop-mediated DNA breaks in cis.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that RNAs do not form hybrids in trans, so that the previously reported induction of Rad51-dependent ectopic genetic instability would be explained by R loop-mediated DNA breaks in cis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all experimental results.

claim: DSBs induced in between direct repeats by DNA:RNA hybrids putatively formed with RNA produced in trans would be repaired by Rad51-independent Single-Strand Annealing (SSA) causing the deletion of one of the repeats.
source: DSBs induced in between direct repeats by DNA:RNA hybrids putatively formed with RNA produced in trans would be repaired by Rad51-independent Single-Strand Annealing (SSA) causing the deletion of one of the repeats.
evidence: This describes the hypothesis being tested, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Other recombinogenic lesions such as nicks or ssDNA gaps cannot be ruled out as initiating events in the SSA assay.
source: A DSB is depicted for simplicity, but other recombinogenic lesions such as nicks or ssDNA gaps cannot be ruled out.
evidence: This is a caveat stated in the figure legend of Figure 1.

claim: It has been shown that it is the length (and the GC content) but not the orientation of the lacZ sequence what impairs transcription and triggers hyper-recombination.
source: We detected a strong hyper-recombination in hpr1∆ cells when the LacZ sequence was transcribed in agreement with previous reports and with the fact that it has been shown that it is the length (and the GC content) but not the orientation of the lacZ sequence what impairs transcription and triggers hyper-recombination (Chávez and Aguilera, 1997; Chávez et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.
